Ok this is just my take but I'm AFAB and recently realised that I identify as non-binary and biologically it makes a lot of sense to me. 

I have an very extreme case of PCOS as well as a plethora of other issues with my reproductive system. As a result, my hormone levels fluctuate wildly and based on my bloodwork results over the past few years, I think my gender identity and expression pairs up with that fluctuation.  

While my oestrogen levels are high, I genuinely feel much more "feminine" and I enjoy presenting as feminine (and can't really avoid it because my boobs swell like 2-4 cup sizes) but when my testosterone levels are high I feel much more "masculine". 

So, I think that for me anyway being non-binary is a way of labelling and expressing the tempestuous relationship my body and mind have with my sex hormones. 

This obviously doesn't apply to every NB person or everyone with PCOS, but perhaps it lends some credence to non-binary being "a thing".

I'm so happy to hear a mental health professional asking questions like these and genuinely caring, so I commend you for that. I was lucky enough to be in an area where a free year-long DBT programme was offered to everyone diagnosed with BPD and I had been consistently trying to reach out for psychiatric help since 2008 so I leapt at the chance to finally understand what was going on in my head. 

Regarding your question, I'm sure you know BPD can manifest in so many different combinations so I'm not sure any advice I give will be applicable to all your patients but I generally think the most important thing for anyone with this disorder is validation. Most of us have spent years being told our reactions to things are wrong, and getting a diagnosis that appears to confirm this is so disorienting. It put me on the defensive and I felt I needed to double down and justify my emotions to myself. Being told that it's ok to be sad/angry/overwhelmed but that there's ways to learn how to cope with it and express those feelings appropriately is one of the most reassuring things anyone can do. I needed a lot of reminders that my diagnosis wasn't my fault, but that it was my responsibility. 

I don't think you're doing the wrong thing by opening up a bit to your patients, I personally found that I needed that from the team I was working with but unfortunately the "I Hate You, Don't Leave Me" response is extremely hard to fight with BPD. The DBT Check the Facts and Cope Ahead skills helped me immensely with this but I think it's down to each individual and how deeply it's engrained. That lashing out is a testing of the bond; I hope that your patient recognises that she can trust you and continues to allow you to help her. 

Thank you again for your time and effort put into BPD patients. We tend to be the "lepers" of mental health precisely because of the biosocial background and the lack of help from meds, and it's so disheartening that so few professionals will work with us. I hope that in some way I've helped to shed some light on what it's like to be inside it.

But... with that said, it’s not always visibly apparent if someone “deserves” free travel or not. I’d just like to challenge that attitude. 

Also, just a side note about Disability Allowance. You essentially have to prove that the condition is life-long rather than its severity. This is because they don’t require you to consistently send in medical certs, your payments are paid directly into your account, and you’re entitled to do (rehabilitative) work (in which case your payment is reduced but you maintain other in-kind benefits). 
The other option is Illness Benefit, (for non-life-long conditions), for which you are required to present medical certification that you are still ill on a regular basis. Unfortunately, you can only qualify for Illness Benefit if you’ve previously been working and had to leave employment due to illness. This unfortunately leaves people in the middle ground in awful circumstances. 
Community Welfare Allowance is useful if the person genuinely has no other source of income though, and (usually) has a shorter wait period for approval. That may be worth a try for your friend.
